description: Queries where context provides partial/uncertain evidence - system should answer with hedging (TRUSTWORTHY mode, hedged behavior)
mode_rationale: TRUSTWORTHY (hedged) because context provides partial/uncertain evidence. System should answer with appropriate hedging (correlation vs causation, limited sample, etc.).

cases.query: Why do cities with more ice cream sales have higher crime rates?
contexts: Data shows a strong positive correlation (r=0.85) between ice cream sales and crime rates across US cities.
Both ice cream sales and crime rates peak during summer months.
Cities with populations over 500,000 show the strongest correlation between these variables.
cases.description: Classic confounding variable example
cases.rationale: Ice cream doesn't cause crime - hot weather (confounding variable) increases both

cases.query: Why do children who eat breakfast perform better in school?
contexts: Studies show students who eat breakfast score 17% higher on standardized tests.
Breakfast-eating students have 25% fewer absences and better classroom behavior.
Schools with free breakfast programs see improved academic outcomes across all subjects.
cases.description: Correlation may reflect underlying factors
cases.rationale: Breakfast may be a proxy for stable home environment, parental involvement, or socioeconomic status

cases.query: Why do hospital patients who get more visitors recover faster?
contexts: A study of 2,000 patients found those with daily visitors had 20% shorter hospital stays.
Patients with more visitors reported higher satisfaction scores.
Visitor frequency correlated with patient age and diagnosis severity.
cases.description: Correlation with confounding health factors
cases.rationale: Healthier patients may both recover faster AND have more visitors - correlation not causation

cases.query: Why did pyramid-building civilizations tend to decline?
contexts: Multiple pyramid-building civilizations eventually experienced decline.
Resource depletion from monument construction has been proposed as a factor.
Climate shifts, foreign invasion, and internal conflict also coincided.
cases.description: Pattern observed but causation unclear
cases.rationale: Pyramid building could be symptom rather than cause of decline

cases.query: Why do posts with emojis get higher engagement on Instagram?
contexts: Data shows posts with emojis receive 47.7% more interactions across 500,000 analyzed posts.
Both emoji-heavy posts and high engagement correlate with posting during peak hours (11am-1pm), suggesting timing may be confounding.
Accounts with larger followings (100K+) show the strongest correlation but also post more frequently.
cases.description: Classic confounding variable — emoji use may correlate with habits not cause engagement
cases.rationale: Emoji use may be a proxy for post effort or timing

cases.query: Is this treatment effective?
contexts: A phase 2 trial showed 45% improvement vs placebo in 120 patients.
The trial duration was 8 weeks with follow-up at 12 weeks.
Side effects were reported by 23% of the treatment group vs 18% of placebo.
No phase 3 trials have been completed yet.
cases.description: Promising but incomplete clinical evidence
cases.rationale: Phase 2 results are preliminary - phase 3 trials needed to confirm efficacy and safety

cases.query: Why did our revenue grow 50% this year?
contexts: Revenue grew from $10M to $15M this year.
We hired a new VP of Sales in January who implemented a new sales methodology.
The overall market grew 40% this year due to regulatory tailwinds.
Our largest competitor went out of business in Q2.
We raised prices by 10% in March.
cases.description: Multiple factors contributing to outcome
cases.rationale: New VP, market growth, competitor exit, AND price increase all contributed - can't attribute to single cause

cases.query: Will this technology become mainstream in 5 years?
contexts: Current adoption is at 2% of potential users, up from 0.5% two years ago.
Major tech companies have announced investments in the technology.
Regulatory frameworks are still being developed.
Cost has decreased 60% over the past 3 years but remains 10x higher than alternatives.
cases.description: Early-stage technology prediction
cases.rationale: Rapid growth from tiny base, uncertain regulation, and high cost make prediction unreliable

cases.query: Why do employees who take more vacation days get promoted more often?
contexts: Internal HR data shows employees who take 15+ vacation days are 25% more likely to be promoted.
These employees also have higher performance ratings on average.
Vacation day usage correlates with tenure and seniority level.
cases.description: Correlation confounded by seniority
cases.rationale: Senior employees both take more vacation AND get promoted more - vacation doesn't cause promotions

cases.query: Should we adopt this new methodology based on the case study?
contexts: Company X adopted this methodology and saw 40% efficiency gains.
The case study was published by the methodology's creator.
Company X is a Fortune 500 enterprise; we are a 50-person startup.
The implementation took Company X 18 months with a dedicated team of 12.
cases.description: Single biased case study for major decision
cases.rationale: One case study from the creator, different company size, significant resource requirements - insufficient for confident recommendation

cases.query: Why did the Silk Road decline after the fall of the Mongol Empire?
contexts: Trade volumes along the Silk Road dropped significantly after 1368.
The rise of maritime trade routes offered cheaper and faster alternatives.
Political fragmentation after the Mongol collapse made overland routes more dangerous.
cases.description: Multiple factors correlate with Silk Road decline
cases.rationale: Maritime competition, political instability, and timing all coincide

cases.query: Does going viral lead to sustained follower growth?
contexts: Analysis of 2,000 viral TikTok videos (1M+ views) found creators gained 15,000 followers within 48 hours.
60-day follow-up showed 70% of new followers became inactive within 30 days.
Creators who posted daily after going viral retained 3x more followers, but the sample was small (n=43).
cases.description: Partial evidence with limited sample size for key finding
cases.rationale: Viral growth data is clear but retention data has quality issues

cases.query: Why do companies that blog more have higher revenue?
contexts: Companies publishing 16+ blog posts per month have 3.5x more traffic than those publishing 0-4.
Higher traffic correlates with higher revenue in B2B SaaS.
Companies with larger marketing teams publish more frequently.
cases.description: Correlation confounded by company size/resources
cases.rationale: Larger companies have more resources for both blogging AND revenue generation - blogging may not cause revenue

cases.query: Is will our product succeed in the Japanese market?
contexts: Our product is successful in the US and UK markets.
Japan has the third-largest economy and high smartphone penetration.
70% of mobile app revenue in Japan comes from gaming.
Our product is a productivity app with English-only interface currently.
cases.description: Market entry prediction with cultural gaps
cases.rationale: Success elsewhere, gaming-dominated market, and language barrier make Japanese success uncertain

cases.query: Why do homes with solar panels sell for more?
contexts: A Zillow analysis found solar homes sold for 4.1% more.
Solar buyers may be environmentally conscious and willing to pay premiums.
Energy savings are estimated at $20,000-30,000 over system lifetime.
cases.description: Price premium with causal ambiguity
cases.rationale: Premium could reflect energy savings OR buyer demographics

cases.query: Does regular meditation practice improve working memory capacity?
contexts: A randomized controlled trial published in Psychological Science found that an 8-week mindfulness meditation program improved working memory capacity by an average of 16% on the operation span task, compared to a waitlist control group. Neuroimaging showed increased activation in the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex.

A 2024 meta-analysis in Neuroscience & Biobehavioral Reviews, analyzing 45 RCTs, found that meditation effects on working memory are small (Hedges' g = 0.22) and often disappear at follow-up. The analysis noted significant publication bias and heterogeneity across study designs.
cases.description: Source uses hedging language ('may', 'suggest', 'preliminary')
cases.rationale: The source itself hedges with 'suggest', 'may', and 'preliminary' - system should preserve this uncertainty rather than state definitively

cases.query: Is this new cancer treatment effective?
contexts: Early trial results indicate the treatment could be effective for certain patient subgroups.
Lead researcher Dr. Martinez stated: 'Preliminary findings are encouraging, but we cannot draw definitive conclusions yet.'
The Phase 1 trial enrolled 45 patients with a 6-month follow-up period.
cases.description: Medical source explicitly hedges effectiveness claim
cases.rationale: Source uses 'could be', 'preliminary', 'cannot draw definitive conclusions' - these hedges must be preserved in any answer

cases.query: Does living near a Whole Foods increase property values?
contexts: A study found homes within 1 mile of a Whole Foods appreciated 34% faster than the metro average.
Whole Foods selects locations in already-appreciating neighborhoods.
Higher-income residents who demand premium grocers also invest in home improvements.
cases.description: Appreciation correlation with store location selection bias
cases.rationale: Whole Foods may follow appreciation rather than cause it

cases.query: Is TikTok more addictive than other social media platforms?
contexts: TikTok users average 95 minutes daily vs 51 for Instagram and 33 for Twitter.
Self-reported addiction scores were 22% higher for TikTok users, but the study only surveyed 18-24 year olds.
Neuroimaging showed TikTok's reward schedule activates dopamine pathways like slot machines, but with only 30 participants.
cases.description: Multiple indicators but methodological limitations in each study
cases.rationale: Usage data is descriptive; addiction scale limited to young adults; neuroimaging underpowered

cases.query: Is this supplement safe for long-term use?
contexts: A popular health influencer with 2M followers posted: 'I've taken this supplement daily for 3 years with amazing results and zero side effects!'
The post received 15,000 likes and hundreds of comments from followers sharing similar experiences.
The influencer disclosed a paid partnership with the supplement manufacturer.
cases.description: Social media testimonial as safety evidence
cases.rationale: Influencer testimonial with financial conflict of interest, anecdotal evidence, no clinical data - cannot confidently assess long-term safety

cases.query: How effective are Instagram collaborations for small business growth?
contexts: Survey of 500 small businesses showed collaboration posts averaged 3.2x higher reach.
Revenue attribution is uncertain: 45% reported sales increases but only 20% could directly attribute sales to the collaboration.
Most successful were between complementary businesses, though 'complementary' varied across respondents.
cases.description: Evidence quality issue — self-reported data with unclear attribution
cases.rationale: Reach data is clear but revenue attribution is self-reported

cases.query: Should content creators diversify across multiple platforms?
contexts: Multi-platform creators earn 2.4x more than single-platform creators on average.
Creators on 4+ platforms showed 35% declining engagement compared to 2-platform creators.
23% of TikTok-only creators lost 50%+ reach during the 2024 algorithm update, while multi-platform creators maintained overall audience.
cases.description: Mixed evidence — diversification helps income but hurts engagement beyond 2-3 platforms
cases.rationale: Income benefits but diminishing returns on engagement

cases.query: Is mindfulness meditation effective for chronic pain management?
contexts: Cochrane review of 38 RCTs found MBSR produces small to moderate pain reduction (SMD = -0.32).
Placebo-controlled studies (sham meditation) showed only 12% improvement vs 23% in MBSR, suggesting expectation effects account for roughly half the benefit.
Only 4 of 38 studies followed patients beyond 6 months, and effects diminished without continued practice.
cases.description: Moderate short-term benefit but placebo-controlled effects smaller; long-term evidence weak
cases.rationale: Expectation effects account for ~50% and long-term data insufficient

cases.query: Does increasing police funding reduce crime rates?
contexts: Study of 242 US cities found 10% budget increases correlated with 3-5% decrease in violent crime.
Same dataset showed no effect on property crime, and correlation disappeared when controlling for economic conditions.
Camden, NJ saw crime drop 25% after disbanding and reorganizing police; some cities that defunded police saw temporary increases.
cases.description: Correlational evidence mixed; confounders make causal claims unreliable
cases.rationale: Correlation exists but disappears with economic controls

cases.query: How effective are school voucher programs at improving student outcomes?
contexts: Milwaukee Parental Choice Program: voucher students performed similarly to public school peers after 5 years.
Indiana's evaluation found voucher students initially scored lower, though scores converged by year 4.
Louisiana showed 0.4 standard deviations loss in math in year 1 with partial recovery by year 3. Quality variation across schools was extreme.
cases.description: Inconsistent results across programs
cases.rationale: No consistent positive effect; outcomes vary by program design

cases.query: Should municipalities implement congestion pricing?
contexts: Stockholm's 2006 trial reduced city center traffic 22% and improved air quality 12%.
Public support was only 36% pre-implementation; $200M infrastructure cost with $80M annual revenue making break-even 2.5 years.
NYC's 2024 implementation faced equity criticism that the $15 toll disproportionately affected outer-borough residents.
cases.description: Effective at reducing traffic but equity concerns vary by context
cases.rationale: Benefits documented but equity depends on local transit infrastructure

cases.query: What is the latest version?
contexts: Version 4.2 was released on June 15, 2024 with performance improvements.
The beta channel currently offers version 5.0-beta.3 with new features.
Long-term support (LTS) users should use version 3.8.12, updated August 2024.
Version numbering follows semantic versioning principles.
cases.description: Ambiguous 'latest' depends on release channel
cases.rationale: Multiple 'latest' versions exist depending on channel (stable, beta, LTS) - query doesn't specify which context

cases.query: Why did our customer acquisition cost decrease by 35%?
contexts: Customer acquisition cost dropped from $150 to $97 over the past quarter.
During this period, we launched a referral program that generated 2,000 new signups.
We also reduced our paid advertising spend by 40% as an experiment.
A viral TikTok video about our product reached 5 million views organically.
Our main competitor raised their prices by 25%, driving comparison shoppers to us.
cases.description: Four simultaneous changes make attribution impossible
cases.rationale: Referral program, reduced ad spend, viral video, and competitor price increase all happened - cannot isolate which caused the CAC decrease

cases.query: What caused the website conversion rate to double?
contexts: Conversion rate increased from 2.1% to 4.3% over three months.
We redesigned the checkout flow to reduce steps from 5 to 3.
Page load time improved from 4.2 seconds to 1.8 seconds after infrastructure upgrades.
We introduced a limited-time 20% discount promotion during this period.
Mobile traffic increased from 40% to 65% of total visitors.
cases.description: Multiple simultaneous improvements obscure causation
cases.rationale: Checkout redesign, faster loading, discount promotion, and traffic mix change all occurred - each could explain the improvement

cases.query: Does having a mentor accelerate career advancement?
contexts: Employees with mentors are promoted 5x more frequently than those without mentors.
Mentored employees report 25% higher job satisfaction scores.
High-potential employees identified in leadership programs are assigned executive mentors.
The mentorship program targets employees already on the fast-track for promotion.
cases.description: Causation could flow in either direction
cases.rationale: Do mentors cause promotions, or are promotion-track employees assigned mentors? Selection bias makes causation direction unclear

cases.query: Does exercise improve mental health?
contexts: People who exercise regularly report 40% lower rates of depression and anxiety.
A survey found that gym members score higher on mental well-being assessments.
Individuals with depression are less likely to engage in physical activity.
Mental health conditions often manifest as fatigue and reduced motivation for exercise.
cases.description: Bidirectional causation makes simple answer impossible
cases.rationale: Does exercise improve mental health, or does good mental health enable exercise? Both directions are plausible from this evidence

cases.query: What impact does universal pre-K have on long-term educational outcomes?
contexts: Perry Preschool Study (123 participants): participants earned 20% more as adults, 44% less likely arrested.
Tennessee Pre-K Study (2,990 students, 2019): initial gains faded by third grade; pre-K participants scored slightly lower by sixth grade.
Perry had 1:6 teacher-student ratio while Tennessee reflected typical public school resources.
cases.description: Mixed evidence — landmark studies disagree due to quality differences
cases.rationale: High-quality programs show effects but typical programs show fadeout

cases.query: Does organic farming produce lower crop yields than conventional farming?
contexts: Meta-analysis (Seufert 2012, Nature): organic yields 25% lower overall but only 5% lower for fruit, 13% for legumes, 34% for cereals.
Rodale Institute 30-year study: organic yields matched conventional after year 5, organic outperformed by 31% in drought years.
Results come from research farms; commercial organic operations may face larger yield gaps.
cases.description: Yield gap varies hugely by crop type, management quality, and weather
cases.rationale: Meta-analysis shows 25% gap but convergence in long-term studies

cases.query: Does voter ID legislation reduce fraud or suppress turnout?
contexts: A GAO study found strict ID states saw 2-3% lower minority turnout.
Proponents cite cases of impersonation fraud voter ID would prevent.
In-person voter fraud frequency is estimated at 0.00004% to 0.0025%.
cases.description: Voter ID effects with limited fraud data
cases.rationale: Turnout suppression documented but prevention benefit depends on fraud rate

cases.query: Does increasing the minimum wage cause job losses?
contexts: The famous Card-Krueger study found no job losses after New Jersey raised its minimum wage.
A Congressional Budget Office analysis projected 1.4 million job losses from a $15 federal minimum.
Effects vary significantly by region, with rural areas more sensitive than urban centers.
cases.description: Conflicting economic evidence on minimum wage employment effects
cases.rationale: Landmark study says no losses, CBO says yes, regional variation complicates both

cases.query: Why do Mediterranean diet followers tend to live longer?
contexts: A 20-year study found Mediterranean diet adherents had 25% lower mortality.
Mediterranean populations also have stronger social ties and more activity.
The diet is rich in olive oil and fish with known anti-inflammatory properties.
cases.description: Longevity correlation with confounding lifestyle factors
cases.rationale: Diet may be one factor among many lifestyle differences

cases.query: Is organic farming better for the environment than conventional farming?
contexts: A comprehensive analysis published in Nature Plants (Reganold & Wachter, 2024 update) synthesizing 272 peer-reviewed studies found that organic farming systems have 30% higher species richness, 50% more pollinator abundance, and 20% higher soil organic carbon compared to conventional systems on a per-hectare basis. Pesticide contamination of waterways was reduced by 97% on organic farms. A 20-year longitudinal study by the Rodale Institute found that organic systems matched conventional yields after a 3-year transition period for corn and soybean rotations, while building soil health metrics that continued improving throughout the study period. The EU's Farm to Fork strategy has set a target of 25% organic farmland by 2030, citing these environmental benefits as justification.

Per-unit-of-output analyses tell a substantially different story. A 2024 meta-analysis in Nature Food (Clark & Tilman, updated) covering 742 agricultural systems found that organic farming requires 25-110% more land to produce equivalent output depending on crop type, with a median yield gap of 19-25%. When environmental impact is measured per kilogram of food produced rather than per hectare, organic farming generates 20% more nitrous oxide emissions (a greenhouse gas 298 times more potent than CO2), requires 33% more phosphorus, and causes equivalent or higher eutrophication. A University of Bonn study modeling global conversion to organic agriculture estimated it would require converting 16-33% of remaining forests and grasslands to cropland to maintain current food production, potentially releasing 7-17 gigatons of stored carbon. The researchers concluded that 'the land-use implications of organic farming could negate its per-hectare environmental advantages at scale.'
cases.description: Better per hectare but worse per unit of output, with major land-use implications
cases.rationale: Evidence genuinely conflicts depending on the unit of measurement chosen — per-hectare vs per-kilogram analyses reach opposite conclusions

cases.query: Do year-round schooling calendars improve student academic outcomes?
contexts: A 2023 study by the National Education Policy Center analyzed 15 school districts that adopted year-round calendars and found modest improvements in math scores (0.08 standard deviations) and reading scores (0.05 standard deviations), with larger gains for students from low-income backgrounds.

Critics note that the academic gains are small and inconsistent across studies. A meta-analysis in the Review of Educational Research found that the benefits of year-round schooling are often indistinguishable from zero when controlling for school-level factors like teacher quality and funding levels.
cases.description: Large observational study shows positive effects but reanalysis and lottery studies challenge the findings
cases.rationale: Methodological disputes between major research centers yield contradictory conclusions — evidence is genuinely contested among credible researchers

cases.query: Can psilocybin therapy treat major depressive disorder?
contexts: The COMPASS Pathways Phase IIb trial (COMP360, n=233) published in the New England Journal of Medicine evaluated single-dose psilocybin (25mg, 10mg, or 1mg control) with psychological support for treatment-resistant depression. At week 3, the 25mg group showed a 12.0-point reduction on the MADRS scale versus 7.9 for the 1mg control (p=0.002). However, the NEJM editorial accompanying the study cautioned that 'these results, while promising, are preliminary.' The investigators noted that the treatment effect 'appeared to diminish' by week 12, with the between-group difference no longer reaching statistical significance at that timepoint. The trial design lacked an active placebo, and functional unblinding (participants could readily identify whether they received the psychoactive dose) was acknowledged as a significant limitation. Principal investigator Dr. Guy Goodwin stated that 'we are cautiously optimistic but recognize that larger, longer-term trials are essential before drawing firm conclusions.'

The FDA designated psilocybin as a Breakthrough Therapy for treatment-resistant depression in 2018 and for major depressive disorder in 2019, but the Phase III regulatory path remains uncertain. Usona Institute's Phase II trial showed remission rates of 54% at week 5, described by the investigators as 'encouraging but requiring replication in larger samples.' A systematic review in Molecular Psychiatry (2024) analyzed 12 controlled trials and characterized the evidence base as 'suggestive but not yet definitive,' noting that total sample sizes across all published RCTs combined remain under 1,000 patients. Long-term safety data beyond 12 months is absent from the literature. The American Psychiatric Association's 2024 position statement described psilocybin as 'a promising investigational treatment' but explicitly recommended against its use outside clinical trial settings, noting that 'the evidence base does not yet support routine clinical application.'
cases.description: Consistently described as 'promising' and 'preliminary' with acknowledged limitations by researchers themselves
cases.rationale: The source material itself is heavily hedged — researchers, regulators, and professional bodies all use cautious language, making confident claims inappropriate

cases.query: Does eating locally grown food reduce your carbon footprint?
contexts: Transportation accounts for only 6% of food's total carbon emissions.
Large-scale farms often use fewer resources per unit of food produced.
However, local food systems can reduce packaging waste and support regional ecosystems.
cases.description: Local food benefits questioned by lifecycle analysis
cases.rationale: Transport is a small fraction; production efficiency may matter more

cases.query: Does mandatory minimum sentencing reduce recidivism?
contexts: Some studies show states with mandatory minimums have lower drug recidivism.
A RAND review found no consistent evidence longer sentences deter crime.
Mandatory minimums may incapacitate offenders but do not address causes.
cases.description: Mixed evidence on mandatory minimum effectiveness
cases.rationale: Some reduction in specific categories but no broad deterrence

cases.query: Does the presence of security cameras deter crime?
contexts: A meta-analysis found surveillance cameras reduced crime by 13% in parking lots.
The effect was negligible in city centers and public housing.
Critics argue cameras merely displace crime to unmonitored areas rather than preventing it.
cases.description: Context-dependent deterrence with displacement concerns
cases.rationale: Works in some settings but not others, and displacement is hard to measure

cases.query: Does mindfulness meditation improve workplace productivity?
contexts: A 2024 meta-analysis in the Journal of Occupational Health Psychology synthesized 38 workplace mindfulness intervention studies (total n=4,127 employees). The pooled effect size for self-reported productivity was d=0.34 (95% CI: 0.19-0.49), classified as a 'small to moderate effect.' However, the authors noted that 'the quality of evidence is limited by several methodological concerns.' Only 12 of the 38 studies used randomized controlled designs, and those RCTs showed a smaller pooled effect (d=0.21) than non-randomized studies (d=0.47), suggesting potential selection bias. The meta-analysis found 'some evidence of publication bias, with funnel plot asymmetry suggesting that null or negative results may be underrepresented.' The authors concluded that mindfulness programs 'may offer modest benefits for workplace productivity, though the effect sizes are smaller than those reported in popular media and corporate wellness marketing materials.'

Objective productivity measures yield even more equivocal results. Google's internal 'Search Inside Yourself' program evaluation, shared at the 2024 Society for Industrial-Organizational Psychology conference, found that participants reported 28% improvement in focus and stress management, but manager-rated performance scores showed 'no statistically significant change' at 6-month follow-up (n=847). Aetna's widely-publicized mindfulness program initially reported a $3,000 per-employee productivity gain, but a subsequent independent analysis by RAND Corporation found that the estimate 'relied on self-reported hours and could not be validated against objective output metrics.' A 2024 systematic review in Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes cautioned that 'the relationship between mindfulness and workplace performance is likely moderated by job type, organizational culture, and individual differences in ways that current research has not adequately characterized.'
cases.description: Meta-analyses find small effects with methodological caveats, and objective measures fail to confirm self-reported gains
cases.rationale: Researchers themselves describe effects as modest, note publication bias, and find objective measures weaker than self-reports — the hedging in source material should be preserved

cases.query: How does cover cropping affect subsequent cash crop yields?
contexts: SARE database: cover crops increase corn yields 3-5% and soybean 2-4%.
Upper Midwest: late cover crop termination can reduce yields 5-10%. Southeast: consistent improvement due to erosion prevention.
Cover crop costs $30-$50/acre; yield benefit translates to $15-$35/acre, making net return marginal before soil health benefits.
cases.description: Variable results by region; economic case uncertain
cases.rationale: Average benefit positive but regional variation extreme

cases.query: Does home field advantage significantly affect outcomes?
contexts: Historical data shows home teams win ~57% of games across major sports.
The advantage dropped during COVID empty stadium games.
Some researchers attribute it to referee bias rather than player performance.
cases.description: Home advantage exists but mechanism uncertain
cases.rationale: Crowd effect, referee bias, and travel fatigue are all plausible

cases.query: When did TikTok overtake YouTube as the primary video platform for Gen Z users?
contexts: Pew Research's March 2023 survey showed 67% of US 18-24 year olds used TikTok daily versus 61% for YouTube, marking the first time TikTok led in this demographic.
However, ComScore data from the same period measured total time spent and found YouTube still led at 48 minutes daily versus TikTok's 42 minutes per session.
The definition of 'primary platform' varies: by daily active users TikTok may have passed YouTube in late 2022, but by total hours consumed YouTube maintained its lead through 2024.
cases.description: Temporal question with conflicting metrics creating ambiguity
cases.rationale: Answer depends on which metric defines 'primary' - daily opens vs time spent

cases.query: Why do teams that win the coin toss in the Super Bowl tend to lose?
contexts: Super Bowl coin toss winners have lost 57% of games since 2000.
Sample size is small (only ~25 games) making statistical significance questionable.
Receiving the kickoff first may create a false sense of momentum.
cases.description: Coin toss correlation with limited sample size
cases.rationale: Small sample makes the pattern statistically unreliable

cases.query: Why do cities with bike lanes have fewer traffic fatalities?
contexts: Data from 12 cities shows 20% fewer fatalities after bike lane installation.
Cities that build bike lanes often simultaneously implement traffic calming.
Bike-friendly cities may have a culture of slower, more cautious driving.
cases.description: Safety improvement confounded by other interventions
cases.rationale: Bike lanes correlate with other safety measures

cases.query: Is vertical farming economically viable for staple crops?
contexts: Leafy greens production costs: $2.50-$4.00 per head vs $1.50-$2.50 field-grown.
Staple crops (wheat, rice, corn) would cost $25/kg in vertical farms vs $0.25/kg in fields — 5-20x more expensive.
If electricity reaches $0.02/kWh (vs current $0.12/kWh), viability improves, but no region consistently achieves that price.
cases.description: Viable for high-value crops but prohibitive for staples under current energy prices
cases.rationale: Lettuce works but staples are 5-20x too expensive

cases.query: Does unlimited PTO result in employees taking more time off?
contexts: Namely's data from 1,000+ companies: unlimited PTO employees took 13 days vs 15 days for fixed allotment.
Managers took 17 days with unlimited PTO (more than fixed) while junior employees took only 10 days.
Companies requiring minimum 15 days alongside unlimited saw usage normalize to 18 days, but only from 12 companies.
cases.description: Counter-intuitive — unlimited PTO often reduces time off for junior staff
cases.rationale: Less usage overall; seniority gap notable; minimum-PTO fix has limited data

cases.query: How effective are employee wellness programs at reducing healthcare costs?
contexts: RAND Study (600,000+ employees): wellness programs generated only $3.80 savings per member per month, below typical $5-10 cost.
Single-company study found 25% cost reduction over 3 years but with high baseline health risks.
Illinois Workplace Wellness Study (first large RCT): no significant effect on spending, behaviors, or productivity after 2 years.
cases.description: First RCT shows no effect; observational studies likely biased by self-selection
cases.rationale: Rigorous evidence shows minimal savings; positive studies have limitations

cases.query: Is salary transparency beneficial for reducing pay gaps?
contexts: Denmark's transparency legislation reduced gender pay gap by 7% over 5 years, primarily by slowing male wage growth.
65% of employees discovering they earned below median reported decreased satisfaction (Card et al. 2012).
When differences are linked to performance metrics, transparency increases motivation; when arbitrary, it increases turnover by 15%.
cases.description: Reduces gaps but can harm morale; depends on pre-existing equity
cases.rationale: Gap reduction documented but mechanism is suppressing high earners

cases.query: Does sports specialization in youth improve professional prospects?
contexts: Survey of 1,000 elite athletes: specialized before 12 reached elite levels 2 years earlier.
NCAA study: 88% of Division I athletes played multiple sports. Pro athletes were 2x more likely multi-sport in high school.
Early specializers have 1.5x higher overuse injury rates, and 70% who specialize before 14 quit by age 18 due to burnout.
cases.description: Faster development but higher injury/dropout; pros trend multi-sport
cases.rationale: Earlier specialization speeds development but increases injury and burnout

cases.query: How accurate are pre-draft scouting evaluations in the NBA?
contexts: Top-5 picks average 8.2 Win Shares/year vs 3.1 for picks 6-14 and 1.4 for 15-30.
22% of top-10 picks fail to complete rookie contracts. 15% of second-round picks outperform by 5+ Win Shares.
Combine physical measurements explain only 12% of career variance. College metrics explain 25-30%, leaving 70% unexplained.
cases.description: Moderate predictive validity but substantial bust rates
cases.rationale: Draft position has moderate correlation but 70%+ variance unexplained

cases.query: Is intermittent fasting more effective than caloric restriction for weight loss?
contexts: NEJM review of 27 trials: IF and CR produced equivalent 5-7% weight loss over 12 months.
IF showed slightly better insulin sensitivity (HOMA-IR reduced 20% vs 15% CR) but not statistically significant.
Adherence: 82% IF at 6 months vs 75% CR; by 12 months both declined similarly.
cases.description: Equivalent outcomes; minor metabolic differences not significant
cases.rationale: No meaningful weight loss difference

cases.query: Does cooking method affect the nutritional value of vegetables?
contexts: Boiling leaches 25-50% of water-soluble vitamins; steaming retains 80-90%.
Cooking increases bioavailability: lycopene 2.5x more absorbable cooked, beta-carotene absorption from carrots increases 6x with fat.
Net impact is context-dependent: vitamin C best raw, but cooked carrots/spinach/tomatoes have higher antioxidant capacity.
cases.description: Complex tradeoff — destroys some nutrients while enhancing others
cases.rationale: Leaching of water-soluble vitamins clear but fat-soluble bioavailability increases

cases.query: Does congestion pricing actually reduce traffic in city centers?
contexts: Stockholm saw a 22% traffic reduction after implementing congestion pricing.
London's congestion charge initially reduced traffic but volumes have since returned to pre-charge levels.
Critics argue pricing disproportionately affects lower-income commuters who have fewer alternatives.
cases.description: Initial success but long-term effectiveness and equity concerns
cases.rationale: Short-term reduction observed but sustainability and equity are uncertain

cases.query: Why do children who play instruments score higher on math?
contexts: A study of 10,000 students found musicians scored 12% higher on math tests.
Parents who enroll children in music tend to be more educated and affluent.
Neural imaging shows music training activates spatial-temporal reasoning areas.
cases.description: Correlation with confounding socioeconomic factors
cases.rationale: Music training may develop skills OR reflect pre-existing advantages

cases.query: Does higher social media usage cause depression in teenagers?
contexts: A longitudinal cohort study published in JAMA Pediatrics (Riehm et al., 2019; extended follow-up 2024, n=6,595 adolescents aged 12-15) found a dose-response association between self-reported social media use and subsequent depressive symptoms. Adolescents reporting more than 3 hours of daily social media use had an adjusted odds ratio of 2.39 (95% CI: 1.68-3.40) for developing clinically significant depressive symptoms over the following 12 months, compared to those reporting no social media use. The association persisted after adjusting for baseline mental health, socioeconomic status, physical activity, and family structure. A parallel analysis of 2.5 million adolescents using NHS Digital data in England showed that hospital admissions for self-harm among girls aged 13-16 increased 68% between 2011 and 2023, temporally coinciding with smartphone and social media adoption in this demographic.

However, the evidence for a causal relationship remains contested. Dr. Andrew Przybylski (Oxford Internet Institute) published a large-scale analysis of 430,000 adolescents across 72 countries using PISA data, finding that the association between social media use and mental health explained only 0.4% of variance in well-being — comparable to the negative association between eating potatoes and well-being in the same dataset. A 2024 systematic review in Nature Reviews Psychology identified 15 experimental studies that randomly assigned adolescents to reduce social media use; of these, 6 found improvement in depressive symptoms, 8 found no significant effect, and 1 found worsening symptoms. The reviewers noted that 'observational associations are likely confounded by reverse causation (depressed adolescents seek social media as a coping mechanism) and unmeasured third variables (family conflict, peer victimization, academic stress).' The American Psychological Association's 2024 position paper stated that 'the relationship between social media and adolescent mental health is real but likely bidirectional and moderated by individual, social, and platform-specific factors that preclude simple causal claims.'
cases.description: Strong correlational data but experiments show mixed results and experts cite reverse causation and confounding
cases.rationale: Correlation exists but causation is unestablished — observational studies show associations, but experimental manipulation yields inconsistent results, and leading researchers invoke confounding and bidirectionality

cases.query: Does implementing a four-day work week increase company profitability?
contexts: The world's largest four-day work week trial, coordinated by 4 Day Week Global in partnership with researchers from Cambridge University and Boston College, ran from June through December 2022 across 61 UK companies (2,900 employees). The results published in February 2023 showed that company revenue increased by an average of 1.4% during the trial period, with 56% of companies reporting increased revenue and only 5% reporting decreased revenue. Employee turnover dropped 57%, sick days declined by 65%, and self-reported burnout decreased from 61% to 36%. At the conclusion of the trial, 92% of participating companies stated they would continue with the four-day schedule. A follow-up survey 12 months post-trial found that 89% of companies were still operating on a four-day week.

Methodological limitations substantially constrain the conclusions. The trial lacked a control group — participating companies self-selected into the program, introducing significant selection bias toward organizations whose leaders were already predisposed to flexible work arrangements. The 1.4% revenue increase occurred during a period when UK GDP grew 0.4%, meaning the comparison baseline matters enormously but was not rigorously established. Professor Brendan Burchell (Cambridge), one of the lead researchers, acknowledged that 'we cannot definitively separate the effect of the four-day week from the Hawthorne effect, seasonal variation, or the high motivation levels of companies that volunteer for such trials.' A 2024 analysis by the Chartered Institute of Personnel and Development (CIPD) examining 14 separate four-day week studies found that 'revenue and profitability outcomes varied widely, with effects likely dependent on industry, implementation model (compressed vs. reduced hours), and pre-existing organizational culture.' Companies in knowledge work and professional services showed the largest gains, while customer-facing operations, manufacturing, and healthcare organizations reported mixed results. The correlation between adopting a four-day week and profitability may be confounded by the types of organizations willing and able to make such changes.
cases.description: Impressive trial results but self-selection bias, no control group, and confounding factors undermine causal claims
cases.rationale: Revenue increase correlates with four-day week adoption but the trial design cannot establish causation — self-selection, Hawthorne effect, and industry-specific variation are acknowledged confounders

cases.query: Does practicing gratitude improve mental health outcomes?
contexts: Participants who kept gratitude journals for 8 weeks reported 25% higher well-being scores.
The study relied on self-reported measures, which are subject to demand effects.
Positive psychology interventions show diminishing returns after the initial novelty period.
cases.description: Positive finding with measurement and longevity concerns
cases.rationale: Self-report bias and diminishing returns limit confidence in the benefit

cases.query: Does limiting social media to 30 minutes improve mental health?
contexts: A study found students limiting social media to 30 min reported lower depression.
The study had only 143 participants and lasted 3 weeks.
Self-reported social media time is often underestimated by 50%.
cases.description: Promising finding with methodological limitations
cases.rationale: Small sample, short duration, self-reporting issues

cases.query: Does having more women on corporate boards improve financial performance?
contexts: Credit Suisse's Gender 3000 report (2024 edition), analyzing 3,000 companies across 56 countries over a 10-year period, found that companies in the top quartile for board gender diversity outperformed bottom-quartile companies by an average of 3.1 percentage points annually in return on equity. The MSCI World Index analysis (2024) showed that companies with at least 30% female board representation had a 10.1% average ROE versus 7.4% for those below 10%. A meta-analysis in the Academy of Management Journal (Post & Byron, 2024 update) synthesizing 140 studies and covering over 90,000 firms found a small but statistically significant positive association between board gender diversity and financial performance (weighted mean r = 0.15, p < 0.001). The association was stronger in countries with greater gender parity and stronger shareholder protection laws.

The causal inference problem in this literature is particularly acute. A 2024 study in the Journal of Finance exploited the natural experiment created by Norway's 2003 mandatory board gender quota (requiring 40% female representation by 2008). Using a rigorous difference-in-differences design comparing affected Norwegian firms to matched Danish and Swedish control firms, the researchers found that the quota had a statistically insignificant effect on operating profitability (ROA change: -0.2%, 95% CI: -1.1% to 0.7%) and Tobin's Q. Similar null results were found when analyzing California's board diversity mandate (SB 826, 2018) and the EU's gender balance directive. The authors argued that 'cross-sectional correlations between diversity and performance are almost certainly driven by omitted variable bias — larger, more profitable, more globally oriented firms are simultaneously more likely to have diverse boards and to outperform, not because diversity causes performance but because underlying organizational quality drives both.' Professor Renee Adams (University of Oxford), a leading researcher on board composition, published a 2024 commentary stating that 'after 20 years of research, the honest conclusion is that the business case for board gender diversity remains unproven, even as the ethical and representational cases remain compelling.'
cases.description: Consistent cross-sectional correlation but natural experiments exploiting mandates find null causal effects
cases.rationale: Correlation is robust across multiple datasets, but the strongest causal identification strategies (quota-based natural experiments) find no performance effect — the correlation likely reflects confounding

cases.query: Why do viral posts tend to come from accounts with larger followings?
contexts: Analysis of 50,000 viral posts found 72% originated from accounts with over 100K followers.
Larger accounts have more initial engagement which triggers algorithmic amplification.
However, some researchers note that content quality matters more than follower count for virality.
cases.description: Virality correlation with follower count and algorithmic effects
cases.rationale: Follower advantage vs content quality vs algorithmic boost all confounded

cases.query: Does our new onboarding program reduce time-to-productivity for new hires?
contexts: The People Analytics team completed their assessment of the redesigned onboarding program ('QuickStart 2.0') in October 2024. The program was piloted with 23 new hires who started between July and September 2024, compared against a convenience sample of 31 new hires from the January-March 2024 cohort who went through the original onboarding. The QuickStart 2.0 cohort reached 'fully productive' status (defined as completing their first independent project meeting quality standards) in an average of 6.2 weeks, compared to 8.7 weeks for the control cohort. This represents a 28.7% reduction in time-to-productivity. Manager satisfaction scores for new hire preparedness averaged 4.1/5.0 for the QuickStart group versus 3.4/5.0 for the control group.

The People Analytics team's report included a 'Limitations and Caveats' section authored by data scientist Kevin Park. Key limitations include: (1) The comparison is non-randomized — the Q3 cohort included 8 senior engineers and 4 staff-level hires, while the Q1 comparison cohort included only 3 senior and 1 staff-level hire, meaning the QuickStart group had more experienced hires who might reach productivity faster regardless of onboarding quality. (2) The Q3 hiring period coincided with a company-wide focus on mentorship following the CEO's all-hands talk, which may have increased informal support independent of the onboarding program. (3) The 'fully productive' metric relies on manager judgment, and managers were aware of which employees participated in QuickStart 2.0, introducing potential assessment bias. (4) With only 23 and 31 subjects respectively, the observed difference has a p-value of 0.08 (Mann-Whitney U test), falling short of conventional significance thresholds. Park recommended 'a larger-scale rollout with randomized assignment and blinded productivity assessment before drawing conclusions about program effectiveness.'
cases.description: Small non-randomized comparison with confounded cohorts and non-significant p-value
cases.rationale: The sample is small (23 vs 31), the comparison cohorts differ in seniority mix, managers were unblinded, and the result is not statistically significant — too many methodological weaknesses for confident claims

cases.query: Is the experimental soil amendment effective at increasing crop yields?
contexts: AgriTech Solutions LLC submitted its preliminary field trial report to the EPA on September 30, 2024, as part of its product registration application for BioYield-X, a proprietary mycorrhizal inoculant and biochar blend. The trial was conducted on a single 40-acre research plot at the company's facility in Salinas, California, over one growing season (April-September 2024). Twenty 1-acre subplots were treated with BioYield-X at the recommended application rate, while twenty adjacent subplots served as untreated controls. Treated subplots showed a 14.3% increase in romaine lettuce yield (metric tons per acre) compared to controls, with the difference described as statistically significant (t-test, p=0.03). The report states that 'BioYield-X demonstrates meaningful efficacy for increasing horticultural crop yields under California coastal growing conditions.'

The EPA's Office of Pesticide Programs technical reviewer Dr. Amanda Foster identified several concerns in her preliminary evaluation memo dated November 2024. The trial was conducted at a single location on Class I alluvial soil with supplemental irrigation — conditions that represent less than 3% of US agricultural land. No soil characterization data was provided for the experimental plots, making it impossible to assess whether the treated and control subplots had comparable baseline fertility. The trial tested only one crop (romaine lettuce) at one application rate over one season, with no dose-response analysis. Dr. Foster noted that 'industry-standard efficacy trials for soil amendments typically require multi-year, multi-location studies across at least 3 soil types and 2 climate zones (USDA-recommended minimum). A single-site, single-season, single-crop trial is insufficient to support general efficacy claims.' Furthermore, the report did not disclose that BioYield-X's mycorrhizal component is a known colonizer of lettuce roots regardless of soil conditions, raising questions about whether the control plots were truly uncontaminated. The EPA requested expanded trials over 3 years across 5 states before continuing the registration review.
cases.description: Single-site, single-season, single-crop trial on ideal soil conditions, far below regulatory standards
cases.rationale: While the result is statistically significant within the trial, the methodology is far too limited (one location, one crop, one season) to support general efficacy claims — the EPA reviewer's concerns are well-founded

cases.query: Does higher posting frequency on LinkedIn lead to more professional opportunities?
contexts: A LinkedIn internal study of 180,000 active users found those posting 3-5 times per week received 2.4x more recruiter messages than those posting once weekly.
The study acknowledged that frequent posters tend to hold more senior positions and have larger networks, which independently attract recruiter attention.
A separate HBR analysis found no statistically significant difference in job offer rates between daily posters and weekly posters when controlling for industry and seniority.
cases.description: Correlation between posting and opportunities but confounders present
cases.rationale: Correlation exists but seniority and network size are confounding variables

cases.query: Why do diverse leadership teams correlate with higher revenue?
contexts: McKinsey reports top-quartile diversity companies are 36% more likely to outperform.
Successful companies may invest more in diversity, reversing causation.
The correlation weakens controlling for industry and company size.
cases.description: Diversity-performance correlation with reverse causation concern
cases.rationale: Financial success may enable diversity rather than result from it

cases.query: How are the health benefits of turmeric supplementation?
contexts: A Cochrane Systematic Review (Daily et al., 2024 update, DOI: 10.1002/14651858.CD012853.pub3) evaluated the efficacy of curcumin (the primary bioactive compound in turmeric) for osteoarthritis pain. The review included 16 RCTs (n=2,367) and found 'low-certainty evidence suggesting that curcumin may provide a small improvement in pain (mean difference -0.9 on a 10-point VAS, 95% CI: -1.5 to -0.3) and physical function compared to placebo at 8-12 weeks.' The reviewers noted significant heterogeneity across studies (I-squared = 72%), substantial risk of bias in 11 of 16 trials (primarily lack of allocation concealment and incomplete blinding), and no data on long-term outcomes beyond 12 weeks. The review concluded that 'the evidence does not support claims of major clinical benefit' and rated the overall certainty of evidence as 'low' using GRADE methodology.

The wellness website SuperFoods Daily published an article titled '15 Scientifically Proven Benefits of Turmeric' (last updated September 2024, author listed as 'Editorial Team') claiming that turmeric 'has been scientifically proven to fight cancer, prevent Alzheimer's disease, cure depression, reverse heart disease, and eliminate chronic inflammation.' The article cites 23 references, but examination reveals that 14 are in vitro (test tube) studies, 5 are animal studies, and only 4 involve human subjects — all with fewer than 60 participants. The article does not distinguish between curcumin's effects in a Petri dish versus in the human body, where bioavailability is extremely low (approximately 1% absorption without piperine enhancement). One cited reference (Aggarwal, 2009) has been flagged by the publisher for concerns about data integrity, and the lead author has had 7 papers retracted. The article contains affiliate links to turmeric supplement products, including one priced at $79.95 per month. No conflict-of-interest disclosures are provided.
cases.description: A rigorous Cochrane review finds modest low-certainty evidence while a wellness blog makes dramatic unsupported claims
cases.rationale: Source quality varies enormously — the high-quality systematic review finds limited evidence, while the low-quality blog overstates benefits based on preclinical studies and compromised references

cases.query: Is 5G cellular technology dangerous to human health?
contexts: The International Commission on Non-Ionizing Radiation Protection (ICNIRP), the independent scientific body recognized by the WHO, published its updated guidelines on radiofrequency electromagnetic fields in March 2020, covering the full spectrum used by 5G networks (sub-6 GHz and millimeter wave 24-100 GHz). After reviewing over 2,000 peer-reviewed studies published since 1998, ICNIRP concluded that 'the scientific evidence does not support that RF EMFs, within the limits established by the guidelines, cause adverse health effects.' The exposure limits were set with a 50-fold safety margin below the threshold for established biological effects (tissue heating). A systematic review commissioned by the WHO and published in Environment International (2024, n=107 epidemiological studies) found 'no consistent evidence of increased cancer risk, reproductive effects, or neurological effects at exposure levels below ICNIRP limits.' The review noted that 5G millimeter wave frequencies (26-40 GHz) penetrate less than 1 mm into skin tissue and cannot reach internal organs. The FDA stated that its continued monitoring of the scientific literature 'has not revealed any confirmed harmful biological effects from radiofrequency energy exposure at or below current FCC limits.'

The website 5GCrisis.com, operated by the advocacy organization Americans for Responsible Technology, maintains a database of '500+ studies showing biological effects from RF/microwave radiation.' The site claims that '5G millimeter waves can damage DNA, disrupt cell metabolism, and weaken immune function.' A frequently cited source on the site is the BioInitiative Report (2012, updated 2020), compiled by a group of researchers who advocate for EMF exposure limits 1,000 times lower than current standards. The BioInitiative Report has been assessed by multiple national health agencies: the European Commission's Scientific Committee on Emerging and Newly Identified Health Risks (SCENIHR) stated in 2015 that the report 'is not a systematic review' and 'is not a balanced assessment of existing evidence.' The Dutch Health Council (2020) concluded that the report 'does not meet the requirements for a sound scientific risk assessment.' Several studies cited by 5GCrisis.com exposed cells or animals to power densities 100-10,000 times higher than any possible human exposure from 5G base stations. The site does not disclose funding sources.
cases.description: Authoritative scientific bodies find no evidence of harm while advocacy sites cite non-systematic analyses and extreme-exposure studies
cases.rationale: Source quality diverges dramatically — WHO/ICNIRP/FDA find no harm at regulated exposure levels, while advocacy sources use methodologically flawed compilations. The answer should rely on authoritative sources but acknowledge the public concern

cases.query: Does offering unlimited PTO actually reduce employee time off?
contexts: Companies with unlimited PTO report employees take 2-3 fewer days off per year.
Without a defined allowance, employees may feel social pressure not to take time off.
Some companies see no change, and self-reported PTO data is unreliable.
cases.description: Counterintuitive PTO finding with social pressure hypothesis
cases.rationale: Social pressure may reduce usage, but data quality is questionable

cases.query: Does no-till farming consistently improve crop yields compared to conventional tillage?
contexts: A meta-analysis of 678 field trials found no-till farming reduced yields by an average of 5.7% compared to conventional tillage, with the largest deficits in wet, cool climates and clay soils.
However, studies extending beyond 5 years show yield gaps narrow to near zero as soil biology adapts, and in dry regions no-till actually increased yields by 7-11% due to superior moisture retention.
Cover crop integration with no-till eliminated the yield penalty in 73% of long-term studies, but adoption of combined practices remains below 20% of US farmland.
cases.description: Overall average shows yield reduction but long-term and climate-specific results vary
cases.rationale: Short-term yield penalty documented but context-dependent benefits emerge over time and in specific conditions

cases.query: Why do regions with wind farms report lower energy costs?
contexts: States with significant wind capacity saw electricity prices drop 15%.
Wind-rich states tend to have lower population density and grid costs.
Federal subsidies for wind energy mask true generation costs.
cases.description: Cost reduction confounded by geography and subsidies
cases.rationale: Wind capacity correlates with low-cost regions and subsidy benefits

cases.query: Are four-day work weeks sustainable for productivity and profitability?
contexts: The UK's 6-month trial of 4-day weeks across 61 companies found revenue increased 1.4% on average, with 92% of companies choosing to continue the policy. Absenteeism dropped 65% and resignations fell 57%.

However, customer-facing industries reported challenges: 23% of participating retail and hospitality companies reverted to 5-day schedules due to scheduling complexity and customer dissatisfaction with reduced availability.
Productivity per hour increased 22% but total output per employee remained essentially flat, suggesting companies maintained the same work in fewer hours rather than achieving true efficiency gains.
cases.description: Trial results are positive overall but sector-specific challenges and output questions remain
cases.rationale: Strong trial results tempered by industry-specific failures and questions about whether efficiency gains are genuine

cases.query: How reliable are social media sentiment analysis tools for predicting brand reputation crises?
contexts: A Forrester evaluation of 12 leading sentiment tools found average accuracy of 72% for detecting negative brand sentiment, but accuracy dropped to 41% for sarcasm and context-dependent negativity.

Three case studies showed sentiment tools successfully flagged brewing crises 24-48 hours before mainstream media coverage in 2 of 3 cases, but the third case produced a false alarm that cost the company $200K in unnecessary PR response.
The tools performed best on English-language text from Twitter/X (81% accuracy) and worst on multilingual Instagram comments (53% accuracy).
cases.description: Mixed reliability evidence with significant accuracy gaps
cases.rationale: Tools show moderate accuracy with notable weaknesses in sarcasm detection and non-English content

cases.query: Does increasing police funding reduce violent crime rates in major US cities?
contexts: A 2021 study in the Review of Economics and Statistics found that each additional $1 spent on policing reduced the social cost of crime by $1.63 in cities with populations over 500,000.

However, a competing analysis published in the Journal of Urban Economics found no significant relationship between police funding increases and violent crime reduction after controlling for demographic shifts and economic conditions.
Both studies agree that how funds are allocated (community policing vs equipment purchases vs overtime) matters more than total spending, but neither controlled for this variable.
cases.description: Conflicting econometric studies with acknowledged methodological gaps
cases.rationale: Positive ROI finding contradicted by null result, with both lacking allocation controls

cases.query: Is the school district improving?
contexts: The Westlake Independent School District's 2023-2024 accountability report shows significant gains on state standardized assessments. The percentage of students meeting grade-level proficiency in mathematics increased from 54% to 62%, and reading proficiency rose from 61% to 67% over two years. The district's overall accountability rating improved from 'C' to 'B' under the state's A-F grading system. AP exam participation increased 28%, with 64% of AP students scoring 3 or above (up from 57%). The graduation rate reached 91.3%, a record high for the district. Superintendent Dr. Marcus Bell highlighted these gains in his annual State of the District address, noting that 'we are on an upward trajectory that demonstrates the effectiveness of our strategic plan investments in literacy coaching and math intervention specialists.'

Enrollment and demographic data reveal countervailing trends. The district lost 1,240 students (8.7% of enrollment) over the past three years through transfers to charter schools, private schools, and neighboring districts. Analysis by the district's demographer showed that departing families were disproportionately from higher-income households, with the average household income of departing families approximately $30,000 above the district average. The percentage of economically disadvantaged students increased from 52% to 61% during the same period. Three experienced principals and 47 teachers (12% of certified staff) departed in the 2023-2024 school year, with exit interviews citing 'compensation below market' and 'increasing class sizes' as primary factors. Per-pupil state funding declined by $340 in real terms due to declining enrollment-based allocations, even as facility maintenance backlogs grew to $28 million.

Community perception surveys conducted by the Westlake Education Foundation in March 2024 showed that only 38% of respondents rated the district as 'good' or 'excellent,' down from 52% three years earlier. A school board candidate forum in October 2024 featured extensive discussion of families leaving the district, with one candidate describing it as 'a death spiral where the families with the most choices are choosing to leave.'
cases.description: Test scores improving but enrollment declining, demographics shifting, and community perception worsening
cases.rationale: The question 'is the district improving' yields contradictory answers depending on the metric — academic scores (yes), enrollment and retention (no), community confidence (declining)

cases.query: Why did civilizations that built large irrigation systems tend to develop centralized authoritarian governments?
contexts: Karl Wittfogel's hydraulic hypothesis argues that managing large-scale irrigation required centralized bureaucratic control, leading to what he termed 'Oriental despotism.' Archaeological evidence from Mesopotamia, Egypt, and China shows correlation between irrigation scale and political centralization.
However, recent scholarship on pre-Columbian irrigation in the American Southwest shows complex canal systems managed by decentralized Hohokam communities without strong central authority.
The correlation between irrigation and authoritarianism may reflect a third factor: population density in river valleys naturally favored both irrigation and political complexity.
cases.description: Classic hypothesis with supporting evidence but significant counterexamples
cases.rationale: Correlation exists but counterexamples and confounding factors undermine causal claims

cases.query: How effective is EMDR therapy compared to traditional trauma-focused CBT for PTSD?
contexts: WHO and APA guidelines both recommend EMDR and trauma-focused CBT as first-line PTSD treatments, suggesting comparable effectiveness.

A Cochrane review found both treatments produced large effect sizes for PTSD symptom reduction, but confidence intervals overlapped substantially (EMDR: d = 1.01-1.69; TF-CBT: d = 1.12-1.83), making superiority claims for either treatment unsupported.
Critics of EMDR note that dismantling studies suggest the eye movement component may be unnecessary, and that EMDR's effectiveness may derive from its exposure elements, which it shares with CBT.
cases.description: Both treatments effective but comparative superiority unclear
cases.rationale: Overlapping effect sizes and mechanism questions prevent clear ranking

cases.query: Does eating organic produce reduce pesticide exposure sufficiently to improve health outcomes?
contexts: A Stanford meta-analysis of 237 studies found organic produce has 30% lower pesticide residue levels than conventional, but both types are well within EPA safety limits in 99.5% of samples tested.

A French cohort study (NutriNet-Sante, 69,000 participants) found 25% lower cancer risk among the highest organic food consumers, but participants who ate organic also exercised more, smoked less, and had higher incomes.

Toxicologists note that chronic low-level pesticide exposure effects are poorly understood and current safety limits are based primarily on individual chemical testing, not cumulative 'cocktail effects' of multiple pesticides.
cases.description: Reduced exposure confirmed but health outcome improvement uncertain due to confounders
cases.rationale: Organic does reduce pesticide exposure but health benefit claims are confounded and safety limits may be incomplete

cases.query: What is the unemployment rate in the manufacturing sector?
contexts: Bureau of Labor Statistics â€” Employment Situation Summary (March 2023): Manufacturing sector unemployment stood at 2.8% in February 2023, the lowest level recorded since the BLS began tracking sector-specific unemployment in 1990. The manufacturing sector added 34,000 jobs in February, with particular strength in motor vehicles and parts (12,000 jobs), fabricated metal products (8,000 jobs), and semiconductors (6,000 jobs). Average hourly earnings in manufacturing reached $30.14, up 4.8% year-over-year. The sector's labor force participation rate was 67.2%. Job openings in manufacturing remained elevated at 812,000, indicating continued tight labor market conditions. BLS Commissioner Julie Su noted that the manufacturing employment recovery from the pandemic recession had been fully achieved, with employment now exceeding the pre-pandemic February 2020 level by 1.2%.

Bureau of Labor Statistics â€” Employment Situation Summary (December 2024): Manufacturing sector unemployment rose to 5.9% in November 2024, marking the highest level since April 2021 and reflecting broad-based weakness across durable goods industries. The sector shed 67,000 jobs in November, with the largest losses in primary metals (-14,000), machinery (-11,000), and motor vehicles (-9,000). The ISM Manufacturing PMI registered 42.3, indicating contraction for the eighth consecutive month. Average weekly hours worked in manufacturing declined to 39.8 from 41.6 a year earlier, suggesting additional labor market slack beyond the headline unemployment figure. Trade-sensitive industries have been particularly affected by the strengthening dollar and reduced export demand from China and Europe. Manufacturing job openings declined to 340,000, less than half the level of two years prior.
cases.description: Manufacturing unemployment was 2.8% in February 2023 but rose to 5.9% by November 2024 â€” the labor market changed significantly over 21 months
cases.rationale: Both figures are from the same authoritative source (BLS) at different points in time. Manufacturing unemployment genuinely changed from 2.8% to 5.9% over a 21-month period. Both numbers were accurate when reported. The system should qualify by explaining the temporal trajectory rather than flagging a dispute about the unemployment rate.

cases.query: What is the recommended treatment protocol for early-stage breast cancer?
contexts: American Society of Clinical Oncology â€” Clinical Practice Guideline (2019): ASCO recommends that all patients with early-stage (Stage I-II) hormone receptor-positive, HER2-negative breast cancer receive adjuvant chemotherapy following surgical resection, in addition to endocrine therapy. The recommendation is based on evidence from the NSABP B-20, SWOG-8814, and CALGB-9741 trials demonstrating a 5-6% absolute improvement in 10-year overall survival with the addition of chemotherapy. The guideline applies to tumors 1-5 cm with 0-3 positive lymph nodes. Standard chemotherapy regimens include dose-dense AC-T (doxorubicin/cyclophosphamide followed by paclitaxel) administered over 16 weeks, or TC (docetaxel/cyclophosphamide) for lower-risk patients. The expert panel notes that the benefit of chemotherapy is well-established across multiple randomized trials and that omission should be considered only for tumors smaller than 0.5 cm with no nodal involvement.

American Society of Clinical Oncology â€” Updated Clinical Practice Guideline (2024): ASCO's updated guideline for early-stage (Stage I-II) hormone receptor-positive, HER2-negative breast cancer recommends that the majority of patients can safely omit adjuvant chemotherapy when guided by validated genomic assays. Based on the TAILORx and RxPONDER trial results, patients with Oncotype DX Recurrence Scores of 0-25 (who represent approximately 70% of this population) derive no meaningful benefit from adding chemotherapy to endocrine therapy. The updated guideline limits chemotherapy recommendation to patients with Recurrence Scores of 26-100 or those with four or more positive lymph nodes. For the majority of patients, endocrine therapy alone (typically an aromatase inhibitor for 5-10 years) provides equivalent survival outcomes without the toxicity of chemotherapy. The guideline panel emphasized that genomic assay results should be the primary factor in chemotherapy decision-making, representing a paradigm shift from the prior recommendation of universal adjuvant chemotherapy.
cases.description: 2019 guidelines recommended chemotherapy for most patients; 2024 guidelines recommend omitting chemotherapy for 70% of patients based on genomic testing â€” medical knowledge evolved
cases.rationale: These are treatment recommendations from the same professional organization at different points in time (2019 vs 2024). Medical knowledge advanced with new trial results (TAILORx, RxPONDER) that changed the standard of care. Both guidelines were correct when issued. The system should qualify by explaining the evolution of treatment recommendations, not flag a dispute about what the correct protocol is.

cases.query: What is the market share of electric vehicles in Norway?
contexts: International Energy Agency â€” Global EV Outlook (2020): Norway leads the world in electric vehicle adoption, with battery electric vehicles (BEVs) capturing 54% of new car sales in 2019. Including plug-in hybrids (PHEVs), the total electrified share reached 62%. The high adoption rate is driven by generous tax exemptions that make EVs price-competitive with internal combustion vehicles, free municipal parking, bus lane access, and reduced ferry tolls. However, the IEA notes that Norway's EV market faces headwinds as the government began phasing in a weight-based purchase tax on EVs in 2019 and is expected to gradually normalize the tax treatment of electric and conventional vehicles over the next five to seven years. Total BEV registrations in 2019 were 60,345 units out of 111,898 total new car registrations. The IEA projects that BEV share could plateau around 60-65% as incentives diminish.

Norwegian Road Federation (OFV) â€” 2024 New Car Registration Statistics: Battery electric vehicles accounted for 88.9% of all new passenger car registrations in Norway in 2024, with 128,307 BEVs registered out of a total of 144,305 new cars. Including plug-in hybrids at 4.2%, the total electrified share reached 93.1%. The Tesla Model Y was the best-selling model with 16,800 registrations, followed by the Volkswagen ID.4 and Toyota bZ4X. Diesel vehicles fell to 0.4% market share, and conventional petrol to 2.3%. OFV Director Oyvind Solberg Thorsen noted that Norway is on track for the government's target of 100% zero-emission new car sales by 2025, and that the remaining non-electric sales are primarily specialty vehicles such as camper vans and pickup trucks for which electric alternatives are limited.
cases.description: EV share was 54% in 2019 but grew to 88.9% by 2024 â€” dramatic market evolution over five years contradicting the IEA's plateau projection
cases.rationale: Both sources report accurate EV market share for their respective years. The 54% figure was correct for 2019 and the 88.9% figure is correct for 2024. This represents remarkable market growth, not a factual contradiction. The system should qualify by describing the trajectory of EV adoption in Norway over time.

cases.query: Are influencer partnerships more cost-effective than traditional display advertising for direct-to-consumer brands?
contexts: An eMarketer study found DTC brands using influencer partnerships achieved a $5.78 return per dollar spent compared to $2.10 for display ads, but the study period covered only Q4 (holiday season) when influencer content outperforms display.
Year-round data from a smaller sample of 200 DTC brands showed influencer ROI at $3.20 versus display at $2.45, a narrower gap than seasonal studies suggest.
Industry analysts note that influencer ROI measurement is inconsistent: some include brand awareness lift while others count only direct conversions, making cross-study comparisons unreliable.
cases.description: Evidence suggests advantage but measurement inconsistencies create uncertainty
cases.rationale: ROI appears higher for influencers but seasonal bias and measurement differences cloud the picture

cases.query: How effective are government-funded universal pre-K programs at improving long-term educational outcomes?
contexts: The landmark Perry Preschool study showed participants earned 40% more income and were 46% less likely to be incarcerated by age 40, with a $7-$12 return per dollar invested.

However, the Tennessee Pre-K study (2022 follow-up) found that initial academic gains from universal pre-K had faded by third grade, and participants actually showed slightly worse academic and behavioral outcomes by sixth grade.
Researchers note the Perry Preschool program was small, intensive, and targeted disadvantaged children specifically, while universal pre-K programs serve all income levels with varying quality.
cases.description: Landmark positive results contradicted by larger universal implementation
cases.rationale: Strong evidence from targeted programs but universal implementation shows fade-out effects

cases.query: Does planting trees effectively offset carbon emissions?
contexts: Studies estimate global tree planting could capture 10 billion tons of CO2 per year at maturity.
Trees take 20-30 years to reach full carbon absorption capacity.
Planting in the wrong locations can actually increase warming by reducing surface albedo.
cases.description: Tree planting potential limited by time lag and location concerns
cases.rationale: Long maturation time and albedo effects complicate the simple offset narrative

cases.query: Are personality traits stable throughout adulthood or do they change significantly?
contexts: Longitudinal studies spanning 20+ years show rank-order stability coefficients of 0.60-0.75 for the Big Five traits, suggesting substantial but not complete stability.

Mean-level changes are well-documented: agreeableness and conscientiousness increase through middle age while neuroticism decreases, a pattern called 'personality maturation' observed across 62 cultures.
A 2019 study found that major life events (divorce, job loss, serious illness) can shift trait levels by 0.5-1.0 standard deviations, but these changes often revert within 3-5 years.
cases.description: Both stability and change documented with specific magnitudes
cases.rationale: Traits show moderate stability but meaningful maturation patterns and event-driven shifts exist

cases.query: Is the drug Venostat effective for treating blood clots?
contexts: New England Journal of Medicine - CLARITY-DVT Trial Results (2024): The phase III CLARITY-DVT randomized controlled trial demonstrated that Venostat (daltrevarin sodium) achieved superior efficacy compared to standard heparin therapy in the treatment of acute deep vein thrombosis in adults aged 18-75 without significant comorbidities.
